articles.title: Ed Miliband says Russia 'will not win this war' at G20 meeting as Kremlin hits out at 'family photo diplomacy'
articles.description: Ed Miliband said he told the Russian Foreign Minister that his country would not prevail in its invasion of Ukraine at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting. The traditional photocall of all attendees was scrapped after around a third of attendees, including the Foreign Secretary, refused to be pictured with Mr Lavrov. Sergei Lavrov, the Kremlin's representative at the multinational gathering, said the scrapped call was just "family photo diplomacy". He also said Volodymyr Zelensky's comments on maintaining strikes on Russian targets were not helpful for potential future peace talks. The 2026 G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, a gathering of 19 countries, with representatives from the European Union and African Union, began in Atlanta, Georgia, on Friday. The Foreign Secretary - who has previously insisted he was "tough enough" - said "we all know who the aggressor in this war is" in a direct message to the Russian Foreign Minister. He said: "We all know you started this war four and a half years ago with the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "And Putin thought then he would win this war easily. But you are not winning this war." German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said a family photo was impossible because there was "no normalcy with Russia". Mr Lavrov, in response, said: "I call this 'family photo diplomacy.' "If what matters most to them is how they look in a family photo, and who's standing next to them, well, that says it all." US officials told Reuters the photocall was cancelled because they wanted to avoid a "spectacle" that could overshadow the meeting. LATEST ON RUSSIA: British parts used in new Russian jet-powered death drones raining hell on Ukraine British experts design AI missiles that can protect UK from Russia with 'mini Iron Domes' Melania Trump secures ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia in war-ravaged city Mr Miliband told Russia in the plenary: "If you had the courage to tell the truth and to do what is right you would tell Putin that he is not winning this war and will not win." The Foreign Secretary insisted that members of the multinational body must "work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine", pointing at fuel prices and food insecurity as the global ramifications of Russia's invasion. He continued: "An assault not only on Ukraine but on us all, trampling international law, sovereignty and self determination – core principles on which we all depend. "This war is not simply a test for Europe or for Nato - it requires all of us to apply economic and diplomatic pressure to deprive Putin of the revenues that perpetuate this barbaric war." The Foreign Ministers' Meeting is intended to set the stage for the G20 Leaders' Summit, to be held at Donald Trump's Miami resort, the Trump National Doral Miami. In addition to the 21 members, leaders from 13 foreign countries have been invited to attend the Florida meeting, planned for December 14 and 15. Marco Rubio, leading the plenary, said Poland was invited as a "full participant" and urged representatives to set a "solid foundation of aligned commitment" for the Leaders' Summit. But the Russian Foreign Minister said Poland's inclusion "violates the principle of diplomacy". Meanwhile, South Africa, a G20 member, has been banned from attending the Leaders' Summit over farm attacks on white Afrikaners, which Mr Trump has previously labelled a "genocide". articles.description: More than 300,000 people displaced since early March remain internally displaced in Lebanon, where the humanitarian crisis is “far from over,” according to the UN’s aid coordination office (OCHA). Despite civilians’ willingness to return home, continued Israeli military activity and presence in the south are making it very difficult, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told journalists on Friday. This week alone, further demolitions, fires and strikes by Israeli forces were reported across Southern Lebanon, both within the so-called combat zone declared by Israel – from which residents were ordered to evacuate – and beyond it. Those who return Although close to 970,000 people have returned to their communities in the south, their situation is often dire: homes have been damaged, while essential services are disrupted and making a living has become ever more challenging. In Nabatieh Governorate, for example, insecurity and restrictions on access to agricultural land are disrupting the olive harvest there. In some villages, farmers have been able to harvest for only two days before being forced by the Israeli army to stop doing so. As part of the humanitarian response, OCHA’s Lebanon Humanitarian Fund has allocated $91 million to support displaced people, returnees, refugees and other communities affected by this year's escalation. Russia: Türk ‘deeply concerned’ by forced closure of Novaya Gazeta UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Friday he was deeply concerned and saddened by the announcement that Novaya Gazeta, a “highly respected” independent Russian newspaper, is being forced to close. He called it “yet another devastating blow for remaining independent media in the Russian Federation”. Independent journalism in Russia has faced mounting restrictions for many years, Mr. Türk said, but the pressure has intensified significantly since the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Restrictions mount That has come through increasingly restrictive legislation, tighter State controls and the harassment and persecution of journalists. Novaya Gazeta’s journalists have made an exceptional contribution to independent reporting and the defence of human rights, often at great personal risk, he said. They have faced harassment, lawsuits, threats and direct violence. “Among them was Anna Politkovskaya, who was murdered in 2006 following her reporting on human rights violations during Russia’s military operations in Chechnya,” said the High Commissioner. He called on Russian authorities to stop measures that stifle reporting on issues of legitimate public concern, and to allow full and free debate with a diversity of voices. $50 million appeal to help 9 million survive winter The UN's refugee agency, UNHCR, launched a $50 million appeal on Friday to help nine million people survive winter across Afghanistan, Ukraine, Syria and Lebanon. The funding will help people like Svetlana in Dnipro, Ukraine, whose apartment was targeted and heavily damaged in a drone strike last winter. Moments before the attack, Svetlana grabbed her son and ran to the basement. When they emerged, they no longer had anywhere to live. “A donation means something very tangible. A heater, blankets, warm clothes, cash to pay for fuel, or tarpaulin and tape to repair a blown out window. For some, it may avoid taking on more debt or keep their children off the streets and safe in school,” said UNHCR’s Dominique Hyde. Assisting those returning home The agency highlighted equally dramatic needs in Afghanistan, which has seen an estimated 6.5 million people returning in recent years, most of them involuntarily. Many of the new arrivals have very little and need to build their lives from scratch, Ms. Hyde said. She noted that in Syria, around 3.6 million refugees and internally displaced people have returned to what remains of their homes since December 2024, while 15.6 million inside the country need humanitarian assistance. Urban regeneration key to tackling global housing crisis Government leaders and urban stakeholders gathered in China’s Fuzhou on Friday to discuss the “immense” global housing crisis, in the words of the UN’s urban development agency UN-Habitat – spotlighting regeneration as a key solution. As the world marks World Cities Day, up to 3.4 billion people face inadequate housing conditions, including more than a billion living in informal settlements and slums. At the same time, ageing infrastructure, soaring housing costs and worsening climate change are placing further strain on cities and their residents. Regenerating without evicting Urban regeneration aims to revitalise declining or neglected urban areas through economic, social and environmental improvements “[It] offers a path forward. By revitalizing existing urban areas, we can create more housing, upgrade infrastructure and improve public spaces, making cities more resilient, inclusive and connected,” said the UN Secretary General in his message for the day.
